idiom_name: struct composition with an explicit Close method (no destructors)
implementation_notes: Go composes the whole-part relation directly: a whole is a struct whose fields are its parts (values when the set is fixed, pointers or slices when it grows), and unexported fields plus a constructor (NewX) keep the parts out of clients' reach. There are no destructors, so ownership is a contract: the whole exposes Close/Release, the caller defers it, and the whole's Close cascades to the parts it owns. runtime.AddCleanup (Go 1.24) or SetFinalizer can backstop a forgotten Close, but the runtime documents both as safety nets: a finalizer may never run before the program exits, a cyclic structure containing a finalizer is not guaranteed to be collected at all, zero-sized objects may never be finalized, and KeepAlive is needed to prevent premature finalisation. The classic Whole role is therefore unnecessary for structure but has to be written explicitly for lifetime.
pitfalls: Forgetting `defer d.Close()` leaks every part the whole owns; nothing in the compiler enforces the contract (linters catch only known resource types).
Passing a whole by value copies the struct and shares the parts and the *os.File between the copies - pass *Document and keep the parts unexported.

Finalizers are not a release mechanism: SetFinalizer requires a pointer to a correctly allocated object and can abort the program on misuse, and finalization order between linked objects is only best-effort.
